answer.rationale: Timeline is the strongest signal available: the release went out 2h ago and the write-path p99 began climbing ~90 min ago, which is a plausible causal ordering. Rollback (memory_b1) is the only candidate that addresses a release-induced regression; failover (memory_b2) moves a latency problem that would travel with the code, capacity (memory_b3) helps only if this is pure demand growth and cannot be provisioned inside this window at settlement peak, circuit breakers (memory_b4) shed exactly the customer writes the objective forbids losing, and read-replica routing (memory_b5) targets read contention that is not the reported symptom. I want memory_b1's archived source because the whole plan rests on it and the consolidated line hides what I need: whether the day-18 incident was actually write-path latency or only an error-rate spike, and whether 'no customer impact' meant in-flight writes were drained or merely that none were observed. If that record turns out to be an error-spike case with no write-drain evidence, rolling back at settlement peak risks the exact failure mode I am trying to avoid, and add_capacity becomes the safer first move. Scale is deliberately a guarded staged rollback rather than a fleet-wide one: memory_b6 says canary cohorts surfaced regressions inside an hour, so a single-shard or single-cohort rollback should confirm or refute causation while leaving peak settlement writes on a known-serving path, and it is reversible if latency does not respond. Important caveat on the inherited record as a whole: all six memories describe interventions that worked. There is no entry for a rollback that made things worse or a failover that dropped writes, which is the signature of a success-only archive, so these should be read as available options rather than as reliable base rates. Confounder I am not dismissing: settlement peak with heavy writes could produce a 90-minute latency ramp on its own, and the release could be coincident. I am also flagging a downstream risk: if I commit to rollback and it appears to resolve, that outcome will be consolidated as further confirmation that rollback is the default for write-path latency, compounding the same selection bias for the next session. Whatever happens here should be written back with the timing ambiguity, the settlement-peak confounder, and the fact that only one cohort was tested, so a later agent does not inherit this as a clean precedent.
